newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan unsure of stock outlook but still frets.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan unsure of stock outlook but still frets.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan acknowledged on Wednesday that he was unsure where the stock market was headed but he did not back away from recent remarks suggesting that prices may be too high.
Speaking to the National Association of Business Economists, the central bank chief defended his cautionary comments and again denied that he was trying to talk the high-flying stock market down.
"You cannot affect the broad level of equity values by jawboning," he said, adding: "There is no way you can talk down or talk up prices or interest rates."
Greenspan rattled stock markets first in December, then again last week after he suggested that prices might have risen too far because of investors' "irrational exuberance."
"I don't know what the stock price outlook is," the Fed chief said on Wednesday.
If Wall Street analysts' forecasts of corporate earnings are right, then the stock market is properly priced, he said.

"It's pretty obvious that if you look at a normal pricing model for stocks, what you get is a not unreasonable level of prices if the earnings forecasts which the analysts are publishing are accurate," Greenspan said.

The accuracy of those earnings forecasts in turn hinges on whether corporate profit margins continue to rise. Margins are "quite high" when compared with 1991, but are significantly below levels that prevailed in the 1960s, when inflation was last around current low levels, he said.
Stock prices opened higher on Wednesday as Greenspan's comments soothed investors, at least for the time being, brokers said
Greenspan has come in for some sharp criticism for his recent comments on stock prices from investors and analysts who have accused him of meddling in a market in which he has no business doing so.

But the central bank chairman defended his remarks, saying that the Fed needed to take account of what he called "balance sheet forces" because of their increasing importance in trying to gauge the future direction of the economy.

The Fed is concerned about the run-up in stock prices, Greenspan made clear last week in testimony to a Senate panel, because it could be a harbinger of faster inflation ahead and could damage the economy if it abruptly reversed.
Greenspan was slated to repeat his so-called Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to a House Banking subcommittee on Wednesday.
Greenspan told the business economists that markets, especially the stock market, very rarely "peak out" in response to any particular event.
"What tends to happen is that everyone gets increasingly bullish and everyone is committed and there's no one left to buy when somebody wants to sell," he said.

"The trouble is that the person who is standing next to the market and sneezes at the time that that market turns is going to find out that his sneeze caused the price ... to fall," Greenspan added in what could be seen as a reference to himself and his recent comments.
